content.v: Fifteen-year-old Jana Green writes about her hobby of birdwatching.

I live in a house surrounded by beautiful countryside in Scotland. I’ve always loved nature and wild animals, and six years ago, I started a new hobby – birdwatching! I went to some mountains in northern Scotland with my family, where we saw lots of birds in their natural environment. I spent hours watching them with my parents, who showed me how to tell the difference between species and how to find the best places to see them. It was amazing, and after returning home, I joined a local young birdwatchers’ club.

My goal is to see 200 different bird species, and I’ve almost achieved that because on family holidays abroad I’ve had the opportunity to see birds from other countries, too. We always look for places where there are group birdwatching activities, so I can add new birds to my list! I’ve been to Egypt, and last summer we went to South America, where I thought I’d have a good chance to see my 200th species. I wasn’t too disappointed when it didn’t happen, though, as I’ve learned that you have to be patient with this hobby.

I posted a video online about this challenge, and many teenagers enjoyed it and commented that it looked like a fascinating hobby. When my teachers saw it, they asked me to give a presentation about birdwatching to the school. I didn’t feel nervous until just before they introduced me and I walked onto the stage. I knew I’d remember what to say and had some notes to help me, but the whole school and all my friends were watching me! I only relaxed when it was over and the teachers said I’d prepared well and they’d really enjoyed it. I might even do another one next year!

I’m lucky to live in the countryside. I understand why many teenagers in cities might not think of becoming birdwatchers, but there are actually plenty of birds to see, especially in places which have lots of green areas. I also think that birdwatching clubs should try to get more young people interested in this hobby. Everyone needs to connect with nature, whatever their age, and it doesn’t have to cost much money.

content.v: Lost Irish beach returns after 33 years

Achill Island, off the coast of Ireland, is a popular tourist destination. It has beautiful mountains and clean beaches. The island was suddenly in the news in 1984 because of something that happened near the village of Dooagh.

They discovered that their beach had disappeared during the night, leaving behind just rocks. For years after that, only small amounts of sand returned to the once-beautiful shore, and fewer and fewer tourists went there.
The effect of this was felt by everyone in the small community.

Then, in 2017, something incredible happened. People couldn’t believe their eyes when, one morning, they found that their beach had returned, and the rocks were once again covered in soft golden sand!
They said that the amount of sand under the sea near the coast had slowly increased. Then, during a period of strong winds and powerful waves, most of it was carried to the shore.
The people of the island were of course delighted to have their beach back, and for some time, it attracted hundreds of visitors.
Business owners in the area were also hopeful that the beach would encourage surfers to return to the region, making it a popular holiday destination again.
No one was sure whether it was absolutely safe.

Later, a special type of seaweed – a plant that grows in the sea – appeared on the beach. It is traditionally used to help crops grow, so its return was particularly good news. The local people are hopeful that now the sand is finally here to stay.
They were able to experience these amazing events.
At first, however, people were advised to avoid going into the sea.
Losing so many visitors meant that many hotels and restaurants had to close.
But a most surprising thing happened that night.
Scientists from an Irish university provided a possible explanation.
Despite these benefits to plants and animals, a few people were disappointed.
One morning, the people living there had a nasty shock.
Tourists wanted to see the power of nature for themselves.
